implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's coroutine forms and adds no runtime: async/await (stackless, Promise-based), generators (stackless, yield/next), and async generators (yield* inside an async function, producing an AsyncIterable). The typing contribution is real: a generator function's return type is Generator<T, TReturn, TNext> and an async generator's is AsyncGenerator<T, TReturn, TNext>, so a consumer's iteration protocol is checked; and awaiting a Promise<T> forces the caller to handle the result. The colour propagation is JavaScript's: an async function calling await is async, and a plain function cannot await - so an async helper cannot be called from a sync caller without becoming async, which is exactly the function-colouring cost. The 'never block the carrier' rule applies to the event loop: a synchronous heavy loop inside an async function stalls every other task, so it must be chunked with await or moved to a Worker.
idiom_name: async/await (Promise-based, stackless) or async generators (AsyncGenerator) for streams; the event loop is the carrier that must not be blocked
pitfalls: A synchronous CPU-heavy loop inside an async function stalls the entire event loop - chunk it with an await or move it to a Worker.
The colour propagates: an async function calling await is async, so a sync caller cannot call it without becoming async; this is the function-colouring cost.
Awaiting a never-settling Promise hangs the request; pair it with AbortSignal.timeout().
A floating Promise (called but not awaited or returned) rejects unhandled - the failure is lost and Node's strict mode crashes on it.
An async generator that is not fully consumed (the for-await loop breaks early) must call .return() on the generator to run its finally block, or the underlying resource leaks.
